newsitem.title: CANADA: Gulf CEO doubts success of CS alliance.
newsitem.headline: Gulf CEO doubts success of CS alliance.

text.p: Gulf Canada Resources Ltd Chief Executive J.P. Bryan said on Wednesday he doubted any strategic alliance devised by CS Resources Ltd could offer investors better value than Gulf's C$413 million bid.

"If they sell 25 percent of the company, are they going to sell at a price higher than what we offer? And then where does that leave shareholders? Is the stock going to stay at that level? I doubt it," Bryan told reporters after a speech to an industry group.
High-tech heavy oil producer CS has said it would soon be in a position to announce a strategic alliance intended to boost the value of the company and thwart Gulf's hostile advance.
Acquisition-hungry Gulf plans to offer either C$14.50 cash, subject to a maximum of C$100 million, or 1.1539 of a Gulf share for each CS share in a C$413 million deal.
Under Bryan's plans, CS would be folded into Gulf's own numerous heavy oil and oil sands assets and offered to the public as a separate entity, whcih he said could be valued at about C$1 billion.

The offering, similar to its IPO of the Alberta government's Syncrude Canada Ltd stake that created the Athabasca Oil Sands Trust, and Gulf's planned issue of shares in its Indonesia subsidiary, would likely be floated in 1998, depending on market conditions, he said.
CS shares down 0.20 to 14.65 in Toronto on Wednesday on volume of 677,051 shares.
Bryan said the current price of CS shares, at just 15 cents above Gulf's offer, was "a good early sign" that investors were warming to its bid.

He said he originally discussed with CS executives the concept of giving to the smaller firm Gulf's heavy oil and oil sands assets -- which include its stake in Syncrude and its 150,000-acre Surmont property in Alberta -- in exchange for CS equity.
But the deal would have been too dilutive to CS shareholders at the then-C$10 share price, he said.

"So we said, 'Look, the only way to do this would be for us to acquire you and then put all the assets into the company and at the appropriate time -- you'd be the judges of when that time would be -- go back to the market,'" Bryan said.
But friendly talks broke off on Friday, when CS announced it adopted a poison pill. Gulf then launched its bid.

CS Chairman Dennis Sharp told Reuters on Monday he believed a strategic alliance deal would help the firm, known for its advanced heavy oil drilling and production techniques, achieve what he called "explosive growth."
Bryan said he continued to hope the companies could return to the table and bring the deal back to friendly terms.

He had hoped Dee Parkinson -- who until last year headed Suncor Energy Inc's oil sands group -- would take on the role of running the combined entity. But neither Parkinson nor Sharp showed interest in working under the Gulf banner, he said.

The heavy oil strategy is part of Bryan's push to move Gulf into a "hub and spoke" operation centered in Denver. The structure envisages the firm's various parts, such as Canadian field operations and international exploration and production, operating independently
Gulf shares closed up 0.05 to 11.90 on Wednesday on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
